## Overview
This method is under development and does not support all of the configuration required for a full timeseries decomposition yet. Cohort comparison is not supported.

This analytics method takes a series of event-based data and uses the Prophet open-source timeseries decomposition library to extract periodic seasonalities in the events.

## Method

1. The event-based data are converted into weekly average event frequencies, i.e., how many of this type of event happen per week
1. The [Prophet](https://facebook.github.io/prophet/) library is used to extract year-on-year trends and monthly periodicity to model the events
1. The trend and monthly periodicity are extrapolated to predict future event rates

## Considerations and Limitations
* We have studied internally how timeseries decomposition can be used to model periodic timeseries data to understand deviations from trends and potientially predict future usage [here](https://adc.bmj.com/content/107/12/e36); however, this method has not been fully validated for all applications. It will require analytics support to ensure the models created are valid and meaningful.

## Example

This example shows how a randomly generated event can be modelled and predicted with this method.

The output shows:

1. The black spots show the weekly number of events observed per week since 2020.
1. The blue line on the top plot shows the modelled timeseries for the observed data, which is also extrapolated forwards past the last observation.
1. The light blue section is the 95% confidence interval
1. The second plot shows the overall trend for the data, which is linearly increasing.
1. The third plot shows the periodic yearly trend, that is approximately 40% high in the winter and 40% lower in the summer.


```{r, example, echo=FALSE, dpi=200, out.width="100%", fig.dim = c(8, 6)}

# Create a random sample of patients in two cohorts and assign random events
set.seed(123)
n <- 30000
df_wst <- tibble::tibble(
  start_datetime = as.Date("2020-1-1") + lubridate::days(sample(1:1004, n, replace = T)),
  day = lubridate::yday(start_datetime),
  prob_cyclical = cos(2 * pi * (day / 365)) * 0.2 + 0.5,
  prob_growth = as.numeric(start_datetime - as.Date("2020-1-1")) / 1000
) %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    # Randomly drop events earlier in the data to make an linear growth trend
    runif(n) < prob_growth,
    # Randomly drop summer events to make a periodic cycle
    runif(n) < prob_cyclical,
  )
driveanalytics::gen_timeseries_decomposition(df_wst)

```
